Boosting Distress Support Dialogue Responses with Motivational Interviewing Strategy
abstract: AI-driven chatbots have become an emerging solution to address psychological distress. Due to the lack of psychotherapeutic data, researchers use dialogues scraped from online peer support forums to train them. But since the responses in such platforms are not given by professionals, they contain both conforming and non-conforming responses. In this work, we attempt to recognize these conforming and non-conforming response types present in online distress-support dialogues using labels adapted from a well-established behavioral coding scheme named Motivational Interviewing Treatment Integrity (MITI) code and show how some response types could be rephrased into a more MI adherent form that can, in turn, enable chatbot responses to be more compliant with the MI strategy. As a proof of concept, we build several rephrasers by fine-tuning Blender and GPT3 to rephrase MI non-adherent"Advise without permission"responses into"Advise with permission". We show how this can be achieved with the construction of pseudo-parallel corpora avoiding costs for human labor. Through automatic and human evaluation we show that in the presence of less training data, techniques such as prompting and data augmentation can be used to produce substantially good rephrasings that reflect the intended style and preserve the content of the original text.

abstract: Diary methods can help us understand how adolescents recognize and manage emotions in their daily lives, which aids in optimizing social-emotional learning practices.This exploratory study invited 30 students to write their daily entries.These unstructured texts were then automatically coded with the help of large language models, which performed comparably to human raters.Importantly, two indicators (semantic similarity and emotional event alignment) were used to assess how an individual's feelings in specific contexts align with the common understanding of those contexts.We found positive associations between diaryderived indicators for positive entries and performance on emotion perception tasks, while students with lower semantic similarity for negative entries showed higher performance on the emotion regulation task, indicating self-regulation in negative contexts.The study highlighted the potential of using large language models to characterize students' daily emotions and preliminarily demonstrated how individual differences manifest in adolescents' emotional lives.

title: Anticipatory affective design in smartphone messaging: A within-AI test of human-reported affective-information availability in requests and invitations
abstract: Initial smartphone messages can be designed around what senders currently feel, what they intend to convey, and what they want recipients to feel before any reply occurs. We conceptualize this process as anticipatory affective design and examine it in requests and invitations. Human participants produced smartphone messages for interpersonal scenarios and reported their actual emotion, intended message emotion, and desired receiver emotion across nine emotion dimensions. These reports showed differentiated affective profiles, indicating that the three affective reference points were not interchangeable. We then tested, within a fixed AI generation architecture, whether message-level design differed when the scenario was supplemented with the same-case Human-reported affective-information block (A) rather than presented alone (N). Three stochastic generations per condition were planned for each of 234 retained cases. Message properties were assessed using source- and condition-blind coding supported by held-out measurement assessment with independent Human coders and an independent-provider LLM. Five prospectively eligible constructs showed positive A−N differences: Recipient Latitude / Response Optionality (Δ = 0.879), Imposition Acknowledgment / Burden Mitigation (Δ = 0.369), Positive Relational Affiliation (Δ = 0.231), Sender Affective Elaboration (Δ = 0.697), and Recipient Support Value / Interpersonal Reliance (Δ = 0.517); all Holm-adjusted p values were < .001. These findings show that, under the specified architecture, adding bundled case-linked Human-reported affective information altered observable message design across multiple interpersonal dimensions. The contrast identifies the total prompt/information effect of adding this block, not separate effects of its affective components, a Human–AI source difference, or recipient outcomes.
